title: Outward rounded interval and ball arithmetic

items.title: Dedekind-complete ordered real field

references.title: Steven G. Krantz, Foundations of Analysis, §1.1, Theorems 1.7 and 1.10

items.statement:
A **Dedekind-complete ordered field** is a commutative field $\mathbb R$ with
identity $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and
the least-upper-bound axiom: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is
bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb R$. Throughout this batch,
all real variables, intervals, limits, derivatives and integrals are taken in
such a field. The integers and rationals are interpreted in their usual
embedded copies. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define $|x|=x$ when $x\ge0$ and
$|x|=-x$ when $x<0$.

items.title: Continuity and derivative on a real interval
items.statement:
For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 15: Derivatives; Laws for Differentiation
Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 16

items.title: Dyadic floating-point format and directed rounding
items.statement:
An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. At finite overflow, a directed result is
the corresponding infinite sentinel and its error bound is $+\infty$; the
status is `overflow`. The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of $\mathbb F$.

references.title: Tucker, Validated Numerics: A Short Introduction to Rigorous Computations, Ch. 1 Computer Arithmetic
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §4

items.title: Dedekind completeness implies the Archimedean property
items.statement: In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, the natural numbers are unbounded above.

references.title: Steven G. Krantz, Foundations of Analysis, §1.1, Theorem 1.10

items.title: Closed real intervals are compact by completeness
items.statement:
If $a<b$ in a Dedekind-complete ordered field, every relative open cover of
$[a,b]$ has a finite subcover. Relative openness means openness in the
subspace topology inherited from the real line.

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 16
Steven G. Krantz, Foundations of Analysis, §1.1

items.title: Nonnegative real square roots exist uniquely

references.title: Steven G. Krantz, Foundations of Analysis, §1.1, Theorem 1.8

items.statement:
In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, every $x\ge0$ has a unique $y\ge0$ with
$y^2=x$.

items.title: Exact dyadic bisection for square-root endpoints
items.statement:
Input: a nonnegative exact dyadic rational $x$ and integer request $n\ge1$.
Output: an exact dyadic lower and upper bound for $\sqrt{x}$; no finite
storage format is needed by this procedure.

1. If $x=0$, return $[0,0]$.
2. Otherwise determine the unique integer $j$ with $2^j\le x<2^{j+1}$ from the
   exact dyadic representation, put $m=\lfloor j/2\rfloor$ and
   $\delta=2^{m-n}$.
3. Set integer indices $L=0$ and $U=2^{n+1}$. While $U-L>1$, put
   $Q=\lfloor(L+U)/2\rfloor$. If $(Q\delta)^2\le x$, replace $L$ by $Q$;
   otherwise replace $U$ by $Q$.
4. Return the exact dyadic pair $[L\delta,U\delta]$. A caller that stores
   these endpoints in a selected finite format must separately round the
   lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up, propagating the resulting
   `subnormal` or `overflow` status.

All comparisons and multiplications in the loop are exact integer/dyadic
operations.

references.title: Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §1
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §7

items.title: Real intervals, complex rectangles and ball enclosures
items.statement:
A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

references.title: Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §§1–2
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §5.1

items.title: Directed dyadic rounding encloses with explicit underflow and overflow bounds
items.statement:
For finite $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, the directed roundings defined in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]] satisfy
$\operatorname{rd}(x)\le x\le\operatorname{ru}(x)$ and each endpoint error is
at most the stated $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)$ (with zero error when $x$ is
representable). For $x>N_{\max}$ the pair $(N_{\max},+\infty)$ encloses $x$;
for $x<-N_{\max}$ the pair $(-\infty,-N_{\max})$ encloses $x$. Overflow has
error bound $+\infty$ and cannot be reported as a finite-error result.

references.title: Tucker, Validated Numerics: A Short Introduction to Rigorous Computations, Ch. 1 §§1.2–1.5
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §§4–5.3

items.title: Outward-rounded interval, rectangle and ball operations
items.statement:
For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

references.title: Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §1
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §§5.1–5.5

items.title: Real and complex modulus product and triangle inequalities
items.statement:
For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

references.title: Steven G. Krantz, Foundations of Analysis, §1.2

items.title: Dyadic square-root bisection gives outward endpoints
items.statement:
For every nonnegative exact dyadic input $x$ and $n\ge1$, the exact dyadic
pair returned by [[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] contains $\sqrt{x}$ and
has width $2^{\lfloor j/2\rfloor-n}$ when $x>0$, where $j$ is the exponent
selected by that algorithm. The bisection loop terminates in at most $n+1$
iterations. Storing the endpoints after outward rounding
preserves enclosure, although storage rounding may increase the width.
For fixed $n$, both exact endpoint functions are nondecreasing in $x\ge0$;
directed storage rounding preserves that monotonicity.

references.title: Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §1
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §7

items.title: Centered Taylor model with derivative-interval remainder
items.statement:
Let $f$ be a real function that is $n+1$ times continuously differentiable on
an open interval containing the finite real interval $X=[a,b]$. Here
$n\ge0$ is an integer, and continuous differentiability means that the
derivatives through order $n+1$ exist there and are continuous. Let $c\in X$
be a dyadic point. Put
$$
P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(t-c)^j.
$$
Supply dyadic intervals $C_j$ containing $f^{(j)}(c)/j!$ for $0\le j\le n$
and a dyadic interval $D$ containing $f^{(n+1)}(X)$. Put
$M=\max(|\inf D|,|\sup D|)$ and
$R=\max(|a-c|,|b-c|)$. The **centered Taylor-model enclosure** is
$$
\mathcal T_n(f,X,c,(C_j)_{j=0}^n,D)
=\sum_{j=0}^n C_j(X-c)^j+
\left[-\frac{M R^{n+1}}{(n+1)!},\frac{M R^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\right],
$$
where products, powers, sums, and the final sum are evaluated by
outward-rounded interval operations. The first term carries input variation
through the polynomial; the symmetric second interval is the explicit
derivative-based remainder. If a required coefficient or derivative
enclosure is unavailable, no Taylor-model certificate is returned.

references.title: Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §11.6

items.title: Cauchy products of absolutely convergent series multiply their sums

references.title: Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I, §2.6.4, Theorem 2.6.5

items.statement:
Let $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n=A$ and $\sum_{n\ge0}b_n=B$ be absolutely convergent
real series. Define
$$
c_n=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jb_{n-j}.
$$
Then $\sum_{n\ge0}c_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $AB$. Thus the
product of the two series can be grouped by total degree without changing
its sum.

items.title: Sum, product, quotient, and chain rules from difference quotients
items.statement:
Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 15: Derivatives; Laws for Differentiation

items.title: Elementary factorial and geometric series converge uniformly

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 22: Differentiating and Integrating Power Series
Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I, §2.6.5, Example 2.6.7

items.statement:
For every real $R\ge0$, the factorial series
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n/n!$ converges. If $N\ge0$ and
$q=R/(N+2)<1$, its tail after index $N$ satisfies
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{R^n}{n!}
\le \frac{R^{N+1}}{(N+1)!(1-q)}.
$$
Consequently the series defining $\exp x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and each of
their formal derivative series converge absolutely and uniformly on every
bounded interval $|x|\le R$. For $0\le r<1$, the geometric series and the
odd power series $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$, with their formal derivative
series, converge absolutely and uniformly on $|x|\le r$.

items.title: Continuous functions on a closed interval attain their extrema
items.statement:
If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and $a\le b$, then $f$ is bounded and
attains both a maximum and a minimum on $[a,b]$.

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 16
Steven G. Krantz, Foundations of Analysis, §1.1

items.title: Power series may be differentiated term by term inside their radius
items.statement:
Let $R_0>0$ and let $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ be real coefficients such that for every
$0<R<R_0$ both $\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|R^n$ and
$\sum_{n\ge1}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$ converge. Then
$F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ is differentiable for $|x|<R_0$, with
$F'(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}na_nx^{n-1}$.

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 22: Differentiating and Integrating Power Series

items.title: Outward-rounded operations are inclusion-isotone and enclose DAG evaluations
items.statement:
For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

references.title: Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §1
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §5.5

items.title: Continuous functions have an oriented Riemann integral

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 18: Integrable Functions
Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I, §5.2.3, Lemma 5.2.7

items.statement:
Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $a<b$, in a Dedekind-complete
ordered field. For a partition $P=(a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b)$ put
$$
U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\max_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad
L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\min_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}).
$$
The supremum of the lower sums equals the infimum of the upper sums. Define
$\int_a^b g$ to be this common value, set $\int_a^a g=0$, and set
$\int_b^a g=-\int_a^b g$. This oriented Riemann integral is additive over
intervals. Refining a partition increases its lower sum and decreases its
upper sum, and any two partitions have a common refinement. It satisfies
$$
\left|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt\right|
\le |b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|.
$$
If $a<b$ and constants $m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then
$m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$; reversing the endpoints reverses these
inequalities. The integral is monotone in its integrand: if continuous
$g\le h$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b h$.
If $g$ is continuous on an open interval $J$ and $x_0\in J$, then
$G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$ is defined for $x\in J$ and $G'(x)=g(x)$.

items.title: Rolle's theorem from attained extrema
items.statement:
Let $a<b$, and let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $g(a)=g(b)$, then there is $c\in(a,b)$ with
$g'(c)=0$.

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 16

items.title: Real elementary functions and their domains
items.statement:
Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

references.title: Rump, Rigorous and Portable Standard Functions, §§5–7
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §7

items.title: Mean value theorem on a closed real interval
items.statement:
Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 16

items.title: The oriented Riemann integral is linear in continuous integrands

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 18: Integrable Functions
Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I, §5.2.4

items.statement:
Let $f,g$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$.
Then $\alpha f+\beta g$ is continuous and
$$
\int_a^b(\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t))\,dt
=\alpha\int_a^b f(t)\,dt+\beta\int_a^b g(t)\,dt.
$$
The same identity holds for the oriented integral when $b<a$, and for the
zero-length interval both sides are zero.

items.title: The fundamental theorem of calculus and integration by parts

references.title: Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 18: Integrable Functions
Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I, §5.3

items.statement:
Let $a,b$ lie in an open interval $J$, and let $f$ be continuously
differentiable on $J$. Then
$$
\int_a^b f'(t)\,dt=f(b)-f(a).
$$
If $f,g$ are continuously differentiable on $J$, then
$$
\int_a^b f(t)g'(t)\,dt
=f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)-\int_a^b f'(t)g(t)\,dt.
$$
Both identities hold for oriented endpoints.

items.title: Range-reduced exponential, logarithm and arctangent series have certified tails
items.statement:
For $|u|\le1/2$ and integer $N\ge1$, set
$E_N(u)=\sum_{k=0}^N u^k/k!$ and
$R_E=|u|^{N+1}/((N+1)!(1-|u|/(N+2)))$. Then
$\exp(u)\in[E_N(u)-R_E,E_N(u)+R_E]$, and the lower endpoint is positive.
For $y\in[1,2]$, put $v=(y-1)/(y+1)$ and
$L_N(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^N v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\ln y-L_N(v)\right|\le
\frac{2|v|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-v^2)}.
$$
For every integer $j$ and $y>0$, the natural logarithm also satisfies
$\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$.
For $|t|\le1/2$, set $A_N(t)=\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^kt^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$
\left|\arctan t-A_N(t)\right|\le
\frac{|t|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-t^2)}.
$$

references.title: Rump, Rigorous and Portable Standard Functions, §§5–7
Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 22: Differentiating and Integrating Power Series
Tucker, Validated Numerics: A Short Introduction to Rigorous Computations, Ch. 1

items.title: Taylor's Lagrange remainder follows from repeated Rolle steps
items.statement:
Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

references.title: Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §11.4
Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 16

items.title: Taylor's theorem with an integral remainder

references.title: Siegfried M. Rump, Verification Methods: Rigorous Results Using Floating-Point Arithmetic, §11.6
Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I, §5.3

items.statement:
Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

items.title: Trigonometric identities, Machin's formula and reduced Taylor tails
items.statement:
The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

references.title: Rump, Rigorous and Portable Standard Functions, §7
Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 15: Derivatives; Laws for Differentiation
Michael C. Colding, MIT 18.100B Real Analysis, Lecture 22: Differentiating and Integrating Power Series
Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §1

items.title: Certified range evaluation for elementary real and complex functions
items.statement:
Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, form the exact dyadic interval $U=2^{-s}X$
without storage rounding. Evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial and
add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|<1/2$, by exact rational interval arithmetic. Round only
the resulting interval endpoints outward, then square that interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece form $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$
by exact rational endpoint formulas without storage rounding, so
$V\subseteq[0,1/3]$. Evaluate the logarithm polynomial and its tail
determined by $\max|V|$ by exact rational interval arithmetic, round the
result outward, and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1,-1/2,1/2,1,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t\ge3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry. Form each reduced interval by
exact rational endpoint formulas and evaluate its polynomial and symmetric
tail by exact rational interval arithmetic before outward conversion; every
reduced argument lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Combine the converted enclosure with
the fixed $\pi$ enclosure by outward arithmetic. Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, outward-round the
exact endpoints $-1$ and $1$; if either conversion overflows, return
`overflow` with the node and input interval, and otherwise return the resulting
interval. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the
quarter-period map for a sine node is respectively
$\sin r,\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r$, and for a cosine node it is respectively
$\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r,\sin r$, where $j$ is the least nonnegative residue
of $k$ modulo $4$. For a negative sign, negate the interval and reverse its
endpoints. Intersect each mapped enclosure with $[-1,1]$. Round the final
endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, form the same finite canonical-cell list even when the input width
meets the wide-input shortcut; do not use that shortcut. For each included cell
$k$, form its reduced input interval $R_k$ as above and evaluate sine and
cosine on that cell. Divide their enclosures only when the cosine enclosure
excludes zero. Otherwise, for odd $k$, form the exact dyadic pole enclosure
$K_k=kP_N/2$. If $K_k$ is contained in the cell's input intersection, then
$k\pi/2$ lies in that cell and is a cosine zero, so return `split-domain` with
the cell. If the cosine enclosure contains zero but this pole test does not
certify a zero, return `inconclusive` with the cell. Take the interval hull of
tangent enclosures only when every piece is finite.

5. For complex exponential on $X+iY$, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$,
and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\ -\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of
$\pi$. Before final outward conversion or hull formation, replace $A$ by
$J=A\cap S_q$, where $q$ is that piece's quadrant. Compute the intersection
by exact endpoint maxima and minima. If it is empty, return `inconclusive`
with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final
conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §§1–2

items.title: Centered Taylor models with derivative intervals enclose the function range
items.statement:
Under the hypotheses in
[[def-centered-taylor-model-with-derivative-interval]],
$f(X)\subseteq\mathcal T_n(f,X,c,(C_j)_{j=0}^n,D)$. For $n=0$ this gives
$f(X)\subseteq C_0+[-M R,M R]$.

references.title: Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §11.6

items.title: Finite-budget validated range evaluation
items.statement:
Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with exactly one designated
output node, an interval/rectangle assignment box $X$ for its input nodes, a
dyadic requested width $\varepsilon>0$, finite-format parameters
$(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$ with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$, series
truncation index $N\ge1$, and integer total box-split budget $B\ge0$.
The supported node types, input assignments, exact dyadic constants and
supplied certified constant enclosures satisfy the admissibility conditions
of [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]]. In particular, every input
endpoint and every endpoint of a supplied constant enclosure belongs to the
selected finite representable set $\mathbb F$. Truth of a supplied constant's
certified inclusion is a mathematical input promise, not something inferred
from its endpoints. Exact dyadic constants need not themselves be
representable; their conversion and any overflow remain the evaluator's task.

Use the following exact membership procedure for each supplied finite
endpoint and for every proposed split midpoint. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$. Compare the value with zero, then enumerate both
signs of $k\eta$ for $k=1,\ldots,2^{p-1}-1$, and both signs of
$k2^{e-p+1}$ for $e=e_{\min},\ldots,e_{\max}$ and
$k=2^{p-1},\ldots,2^p-1$, stopping at a match. If the finite enumeration
ends without a match, report `not-in-format`. Every comparison is an exact
dyadic equality test. This is the representable set of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]], including zero
and subnormals. Before initializing the queue, check the integer/format
conditions and the finite input and supplied-constant endpoint memberships;
malformed data or a failed membership returns `inconclusive` with the
identifying input status, without an evaluator call. An empty input returns
`empty` as in the elementary evaluator.

Keep the DAG, designated output, constant enclosures, format and $N$ fixed.
Set a shared counter $R:=B$ and a queue containing $X$. Process the queue in
first-in, first-out order. For each box $Q$, evaluate the DAG by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with the same format and $N$,
requesting only the designated output node's enclosure. The hull of no
completed leaves is recorded as `empty`.

- If evaluation returns a non-finite status, return that status and the exact
  unresolved box $Q$; it is not a tolerance certificate.
- If it returns a finite enclosure $I$ with width at most $\varepsilon$, save
  $I$ as a completed leaf enclosure.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R=0$, return
  `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, $Q$, and the unmet width test.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R>0$, select
  a widest nondegenerate input coordinate (breaking ties by the first
  coordinate in the input order). If there is no such coordinate, return
  `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, the unresolved parent $Q$,
  the remaining queue, and status `no-splittable-coordinate` with the unmet
  width test. Otherwise compute its midpoint $m$ by exact dyadic arithmetic
  and apply the membership procedure above in the actual selected format.
  If it reports `not-in-format`, return `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf
  hull, the unresolved parent $Q$, the remaining queue, and status
  `midpoint-not-in-format`, identifying the coordinate and exact midpoint.
  Do not enqueue either child or call the evaluator on it in this case.
  If $m\in\mathbb F$, split that coordinate into the two closed halves at
  $m$, decrement $R$ by one, and append both children to the queue.

When the queue is empty, take the hull $J$ of all completed leaf enclosures.
Return `certified(J,X)` only if $\operatorname{width}(J)\le\varepsilon$;
otherwise return `inconclusive(J,X)` and state that the global width test
failed.

items.title: Certified real elementary-function evaluations enclose their ranges
items.statement:
Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

references.title: Rump, Rigorous and Portable Standard Functions, §§5–7
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §§5–8

items.title: Certified complex exponential and principal logarithm enclose their ranges
items.statement:
For any finite complex rectangle on which the principal branch is defined,
every finite output of [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for
$\exp$ or $\operatorname{Log}$ contains the exact image. For nested rectangles
within the same admissible branch, the canonical quadrant subdivision and
outward operations preserve inclusion. Rectangles meeting zero, the negative
real branch cut, or an unresolved quadrant return the declared domain or
inconclusive status.

references.title: Rump, Rigorous and Portable Standard Functions, §10
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §§5.1–5.5 and 7

items.title: Budgeted range evaluation terminates and certifies only sound enclosures
items.statement:
For every finite input DAG and finite total split budget $B$, the algorithm
[[alg-budgeted-validated-range-evaluation]] terminates. If it returns
`certified(I,X)`, then $I$ contains the exact function range on all of $X$ and
has width at most the requested $\varepsilon$. If it returns `empty`,
`entire`, `inconclusive`, domain error, split-domain, or overflow, it makes no
unconditional tolerance-success claim.

Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §8.3

title: Outward rounded interval and ball arithmetic — Examples

items.title: Division of [1,2] by [-1,1] has no finite hull
items.statement:
Take numerator interval $X=[1,2]$ and divisor interval $Y=[-1,1]$. The exact
quotient set over $y\ne0$ is unbounded above and below. Therefore no finite
interval is a sound hull; the permitted results are a sign split or an
`entire`/`inconclusive` status.

references.title: Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §1
Rump, Verification methods: Rigorous results using floating-point arithmetic, §§5.1 and 5.4

items.title: Natural interval subtraction loses repeated-input correlation
items.statement:
Let the single real input $x$ range over $X=[1,2]$, and evaluate the expression
DAG $f(x)=x-x$ by its natural interval extension. The exact range is
$f(X)=\{0\}$, while the interval computation returns $X-X=[-1,1]$. Both
endpoints are sound, but the output is wider because the two occurrences of
$x$ are evaluated as independent members of $X$.

references.title: Kearfott, Interval Computations: Introduction, Uses, and Resources, §1

items.title: Certified sine range near a multiple of pi
items.statement:
Use truncation index $N=12$ (13 retained terms) and the finite format
$p=128$, $e_{\min}=-512$, $e_{\max}=512$. Form the Machin interval $P$
from exact rational partial
sums and the alternating-series tail bounds, and round only its final two
endpoints outward. The formula in the trigonometric lemma gives
$$
\operatorname{width}(P)\le
\frac{32(1/5)^{27}}{27(1-1/25)}+
\frac{8(1/239)^{27}}{27(1-1/239^2)}+2\cdot2^{-126}<10^{-18}.
$$
Let $X=2P$, request width $\varepsilon=1$, and use total box-split budget
$B=0$. The certified sine evaluator uses the canonical cell $k=4$ and the
range reduction centered at $2\pi$.
